name: MODY type 2 (GCK)
aliases: glucokinase-related maturity-onset diabetes of the young

reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous inactivating mutations in GCK, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance
Characterised by mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia that is usually present from birth and often discovered incidentally
Fasting glucose typically sits in a narrow, modestly elevated range and HbA1c remains only slightly above the reference limit
The glucose increment during an oral glucose tolerance test is characteristically small because the glucose sensor is merely reset to a higher threshold
Most individuals do not require pharmacological treatment and are managed by observation rather than glucose-lowering therapy
Microvascular and macrovascular complications are rare, reflecting the mild lifelong glycaemic elevation
Pregnancy is the key exception: management depends on whether the fetus has inherited the mutation, which influences fetal growth
reference.pathophysiology: Glucokinase acts as the glucose sensor of the pancreatic beta cell, phosphorylating glucose and thereby setting the threshold at which insulin secretion is triggered. Heterozygous inactivating GCK mutations raise this set point, so insulin release occurs at a higher-than-normal glucose concentration. The result is a regulated, mildly elevated fasting glucose that the body defends around a new equilibrium rather than a progressive failure of insulin secretion. Because glucose homeostasis is otherwise intact, hyperglycaemia remains stable across life and complications are uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Gestational diabetes when first detected in pregnancy
Impaired fasting glucose of multifactorial origin
additionalInvestigations: Fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c demonstrating mild, stable elevation
Oral glucose tolerance test showing a small glucose increment
Molecular genetic testing of GCK to confirm the diagnosis
Negative pancreatic autoantibodies to help exclude type 1 diabetes
Family glucose screening across generations to demonstrate the dominant pattern
redFlags: Rapidly worsening hyperglycaemia or ketosis, which is inconsistent with GCK-MODY and suggests an alternative diagnosis
Marked postprandial glucose excursions pointing away from the stable phenotype
Symptoms of osmotic diuresis or weight loss indicating another cause of diabetes
Emergence of significant complications, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with lifelong mild stable hyperglycaemia that rarely leads to diabetes-related complications and generally does not require pharmacological treatment.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the condition as type 1 or type 2 diabetes and starting unnecessary insulin or oral agents
Interpreting a persistently mild HbA1c as poorly controlled diabetes requiring escalation
Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history that points to a monogenic cause
Failing to consider fetal genotype when planning management in pregnancy
management: Manage most non-pregnant patients with lifestyle measures alone, as no glucose-lowering drug is required for this reset glucose set-point
Withhold and, where started, withdraw unnecessary pharmacotherapy and intensive monitoring after GCK-MODY is genetically confirmed
In pregnancy, base treatment on foetal genotype, offering insulin for an unaffected macrosomic foetus and avoiding intensive treatment when the foetus is affected
Perform serial foetal growth ultrasound in affected pregnancies
Reassure that clinically significant diabetic complications are rare and tight glycaemic targets are unnecessary
Offer genetic counselling and cross-generational family screening for autosomal dominant inheritance
